title: Comparing Large Language Model AI and Human-Generated Coaching Messages for Behavioral Weight Loss
venue: Journal of Technology in Behavioral Science
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language model (LLM) artificial intelligence, specifically ChatGPT, can generate behavioral weight loss coaching messages that are perceived as helpful as those written by a human coach. The authors address a practical problem in automated health coaching: existing rule-based or templated messages can feel repetitive, impersonal, and costly to scale, potentially limiting engagement and effectiveness.

The study used messages drawn from an ongoing year-long behavioral weight-loss trial (Project ReLearn) involving adults in the United States with overweight or obesity. Eighty-seven participants rated ten coaching messages across two phases: five human-written and five ChatGPT-generated messages. After Phase 1 feedback suggested the AI messages felt impersonal, overly negative, and overly data-driven, the prompt was revised to better convey empathy and encouragement, and a second set of messages was generated for Phase 2. Participants rated helpfulness, judged whether messages were AI- or human-written, and provided open-ended feedback.

Quantitatively, ChatGPT messages improved from Phase 1 to Phase 2 and were rated nearly as helpful as human-written messages by the end of the study, though human messages still held a small advantage. Participants often could not reliably distinguish AI from human messages, suggesting the model could mimic human-like coaching fairly well. Qualitatively, however, participants preferred messages that felt more authentic, personalized, autonomy-supportive, and context-aware, and they were wary of formulaic, overly prescriptive, or overly enthusiastic wording. The authors conclude that LLMs show promise for scalable weight-loss coaching, but further prompt refinement and future trials are needed to evaluate actual clinical effectiveness.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed, small-sample comparative study with mixed quantitative and qualitative methods, but it is not an RCT and does not evaluate real-world outcomes beyond subjective ratings. It provides useful early evidence but has notable concerns about ecological validity and generalizability.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest-to-moderate perceived helpfulness gains after prompt refinement (e.g., d=0.15 in Phase 2 human-vs-AI comparison), but the outcome is subjective and limited to a weight-loss coaching context. The practical impact is promising but still unclear for broader deployment or behavioral outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) generated behavioral weight-loss coaching messages from structured participant data and prompts, with prompt refinement across two phases to improve tone, empathy, and helpfulness.

finding.finding_summary: Participants rated ChatGPT-generated coaching messages as less helpful than human-written messages in Phase 1 (median 3 vs 4; t(234)=8.41, p<0.001, d=0.55), but after prompt revisions in Phase 2 the gap narrowed substantially (median 4 vs 4; t(199)=2.10, p=0.037, d=0.15). Qualitative feedback indicated the AI messages were more empathetic and personalized in Phase 2, yet still often felt formulaic, impersonal, and overly prescriptive.
finding.measure: Perceived helpfulness ratings of coaching messages on a 1–5 Likert scale; open-ended participant feedback
finding.effect_size: d=0.55 (Phase 1 human vs AI); d=0.15 (Phase 2 human vs AI); d=0.48 (AI improvement from Phase 1 to Phase 2)
